text: A fix nobody wrote down is a fix nobody can learn from -- including future-you, six months from now, staring at IX_Orders_CustomerID_OrderDate wondering why it exists. T-SQL for Database Administrators built a habit of documenting what you find; this lesson applies that habit to a real tuning write-up, for a real audience.

A manager skimming a status channel and a DBA debugging this table in a year want different depths of the same information. Five short sections cover both. Summary: one or two sentences, no jargon -- Order History lookups for high-volume wholesale accounts were timing out during peak hours, root cause was a missing covering index, fixed and verified on the date. Symptom: what was actually reported -- the panel timing out after thirty seconds for certain accounts, worst ten AM to two PM, starting about six weeks prior. Root cause: the specific technical finding -- IX_Orders_CustomerID didn't cover the query, causing a Key Lookup per row, eighteen thousand four hundred of them for TrailWorks Co-op, driving dominant PAGEIOLATCH_SH waits at peak concurrency.

Change made: the exact CREATE INDEX and DROP INDEX statements from Lesson 49, verbatim, not paraphrased -- anyone auditing this change later needs the real T-SQL. Result: the verified numbers from Lesson 50 -- duration about twenty-eight thousand milliseconds down to about eighty-five, logical reads about a hundred eighteen thousand down to about three hundred fifty, PAGEIOLATCH_SH waits effectively eliminated, no measurable write-side regression. The manager-facing version leans on summary and result; the DBA-facing version leans on root cause and change made. Same underlying facts, two depths, never two different stories.

The change-made section records the real statements verbatim: CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_CustomerID_OrderDate on dbo dot Orders, keyed on CustomerID and OrderDate descending, including OrderStatus, OrderTotal, and ShipDate -- followed by DROP INDEX IX_Orders_CustomerID. Anything ambiguous that a future investigation should know goes here too: this covering index solves usp_CustomerOrderHistory specifically, and a different report against dbo dot Orders would need its own covering index, not an assumption that this one already covers it.

Six months from now, we added an index tells nobody anything useful. We added it because the existing index didn't include the columns the query selected, and Key Lookups scale with order count, is a finding the next DBA can actually reuse on a different procedure. Documentation that only records what was changed expires the moment someone forgets why. Documentation that records the reasoning keeps paying off.
